standard.title: Spatial variations in wellbeing in Australia
standard.description: reasons for, and consequences of, spatial variations in human wellbeing in Australia, including for First Nations Australians
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand spatial wellbeing variations at the regional/national scale using international cases (AC9HG10K06) and are familiar with wellbeing measurement tools (AC9HG10K05). They have engaged with First Nations custodial approaches (AC9HG10K03) and Australia's internal migration and urban/rural dynamics (AC9HG8K06, AC9HG8K08).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the reasons for and consequences of spatial variations in human wellbeing in Australia, including identifying causes for First Nations Australians' wellbeing data and explaining how a person's wellbeing is influenced by where they live, with reference to interconnections of environmental, economic, social and technological factors in at least two different places.

nodes.label: Spatial patterns of wellbeing in Australia
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the spatial pattern of wellbeing variation within Australia, identifying areas of higher and lower wellbeing and recognising the particular pattern for First Nations Australians.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe wellbeing variation across at least two different Australian places (e.g. urban and remote) using at least one data source.
nodes.typical_width: Interpret and analyse similarities, differences, patterns and trends in wellbeing data across Australian places including urban, regional and remote; identify the particular wellbeing profile of First Nations Australians compared to non-Indigenous Australians.
wider: Map spatial wellbeing data across Australian states/territories or statistical areas, identifying clustering patterns and geographic gradients
Examine how wellbeing data for First Nations Australians varies within the First Nations population — for example, between urban, regional and remote communities — avoiding a single national average
Trace how the spatial distribution of wellbeing in Australia has changed over recent decades, identifying which regions have experienced improvement and which have stagnated
nodes.hinge_reason: The spatial pattern provides the foundation for cause identification — if students do not first establish what the pattern is and where the variation sits geographically, their causal explanations will be generic rather than place-specific.

response_modes.reason: Students often jump to causes (remote areas are disadvantaged because they are far away) without first establishing the data picture. Scaffold data reading before explanation — what does the data actually show about spatial variation?

success_criteria: Students describe the spatial distribution of wellbeing in Australia, identifying at least two geographically distinct places with different wellbeing profiles
Students identify the wellbeing gap between First Nations and non-Indigenous Australians using at least one specific data point or measure

nodes.label: Causes of wellbeing variation — environmental, economic, social, technological
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the environmental, social, economic and technological factors that influence wellbeing and create spatial variation across Australian places, including factors specific to First Nations Australians' wellbeing.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify and explain at least two factors from different domains (e.g. one economic, one social) that contribute to wellbeing variation between two Australian places.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how environmental (access to resources, climate), social (health and education services), economic (employment, income) and technological (ICT access) factors interact to create wellbeing variation across Australian places; explain the additional and intersecting factors that shape First Nations Australians' wellbeing, including Closing the Gap initiatives.
wider: Investigate how historical policies (stolen generations, land alienation, forced relocation) created structural disadvantages that persist as causes of current wellbeing gaps for First Nations Australians
Examine the concept of the 'tyranny of distance' as a driver of regional disadvantage in Australia and evaluate policy responses that have attempted to address it
Analyse a specific remote community's wellbeing profile and trace the full factor set — geographical, historical, economic, social — that produces that profile

response_modes.reason: Factor analysis is enriched by comparing two very different Australian places — e.g. a remote First Nations community vs an outer suburban area vs a regional town — to show that the same factor domain (e.g. economic) operates very differently in different geographic contexts.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The multi-factor analysis across diverse Australian place types is substantively rich — each place type involves a different combination of drivers, and students who have traced causes in at least two contrasting places develop a more nuanced causal framework.
success_criteria: Students explain at least two factors from different domains (environmental, economic, social, technological) that contribute to wellbeing variation between named Australian places
Students explain at least one factor specific to First Nations Australians' wellbeing, connecting it to a historical or structural cause

nodes.label: Place, interconnection and wellbeing outcomes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how a person's wellbeing is influenced by where they live, with reference to interconnections of environmental, economic, social and technological factors in at least two different Australian places.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how interconnections between at least two factors (e.g. economic and social) shape wellbeing outcomes for people in one specific Australian place.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how a person's wellbeing is shaped by their place through the interconnection of environmental, economic, social and technological factors; demonstrate this for at least two different Australian places, including consideration of ways to improve wellbeing of remote First Nations communities including community-proposed approaches.
wider: Develop a detailed interconnection web for a specific place showing how multiple factors interact and compound — identifying which factor interactions are most significant for wellbeing outcomes
Investigate and evaluate specific strategies proposed or implemented by First Nations communities themselves to improve wellbeing, assessing how community agency shapes outcomes

Compare how two different government policy approaches to regional wellbeing in Australia have fared — for example, comparing place-based investment strategies with targeted individual support schemes

response_modes.reason: This node integrates spatial pattern reading, factor analysis and the geographical concept of place into a holistic account of wellbeing as place-shaped. Students need to connect the factors identified in Node 2 into a coherent explanation of how interconnections produce a place-specific wellbeing outcome.
The descriptor requires at least two different places — the comparison is integral, not optional. Teaching should ensure students have genuine comparative material, not just a single case study.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Place-based interconnection analysis is the culminating skill for the wellbeing strand. Students who have genuinely compared two or more contrasting Australian places develop a more portable analytical framework for applying place-based thinking.
success_criteria: Students explain how at least two interconnected factors shape a person's wellbeing in a specific Australian place
Students identify how the wellbeing experience differs between at least two different Australian places and explain the geographical basis of that difference
